clue.text: Hit celebrated late in to the night

definitions.meaning: to hit someone with a heavy stick or cudgel

definitions.text: celebrated late in to the night
definitions.meaning: partied at nightclubs until the small hours

explanation.surface: Someone was struck after partying into the small hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share one word: beaten with a cudgel, and having spent the night going round nightclubs.

clue.text: Put cover over well, like an old hand

parts.note: to cap something is to put a lid or covering on it
doing something well is doing it ably

explanation.surface: Someone lids a well neatly, like a seasoned worker.
explanation.definitionFit: An old hand is an experienced person, who does things competently and skilfully.

clue.text: Works turning up in college were the first preserved intact

indicators.note: in places the turned word inside the college word

parts.note: uni is the informal word for a university or college

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word for works is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: opera are works; OPS is the abbreviation for opuses
those who were first led the field

explanation.surface: Musical works resurfacing in a college library were the earliest to survive undamaged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' stands for opus numbers, abbreviated; 'turning up' works only because this is a down clue, read from the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unspoiled has been kept whole and undamaged, the same as preserved intact.

clue.text: 14 wrote this line, following shortage in pub

indicators.note: following places the line word after the rest
in puts the shortage word inside the pub word

parts.note: a bar is a pub
a lack is a shortage
a row is a line

explanation.surface: A writer penned a line about a pub running short of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 is STEVENSON, Robert Louis Stevenson, whose novel 'The Black Arrow' appeared in 1888.
explanation.definitionFit: The Black Arrow is an adventure novel by Robert Louis Stevenson, set in the Wars of the Roses.

clue.text: Key European sets limits on chosen representatives

parts.note: DEL is the delete key on a keyboard
to gate someone, as at a British boarding school, is to confine them to grounds

explanation.surface: A leading European restricts the people elected to speak for others.
explanation.walkthrough: Gating is a British school punishment: a pupil who is gated may not leave the premises.
explanation.definitionFit: Delegates are people selected to act or vote on behalf of a group at a meeting.

clue.text: Occupied area in Kent, roughly on the way to London

indicators.note: in puts the area letter inside the rearranged county
roughly says the county name is shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
travelling up is the British convention for heading to the capital

explanation.surface: Somewhere in Kent is settled, conveniently on the road up to London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' turns KENT into TKEN; A goes inside to give TAKEN. Kent is a county south-east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Time or space that is taken up has been filled or used, so it is occupied.

clue.text: Some rejected these maths disciplines

indicators.note: rejected says the hidden letters are read backwards
Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Pupils reject the parts of mathematics they are taught.
explanation.walkthrough: SEMAT, found inside 'these maths', is turned round by 'rejected'.
explanation.definitionFit: To discipline is to bring under control, as one does in taming an animal; both verbs mean subdue.

clue.text: Dropped off bottles and upset 14's work

indicators.note: bottles means holds inside, as a bottle holds its contents

parts.note: to kip is to sleep, so someone who dropped off kipped

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the little word 'and' upside down

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone dozed off, holding something, and wrecked a writer's book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns AND into DNA, which the sleep word holds. 14 is Robert Louis Stevenson.
explanation.definitionFit: Kidnapped is Robert Louis Stevenson's 1886 novel about David Balfour, a work by that author.

clue.text: More charming king shunned by cooler queen

indicators.note: shunned by says the king letter is left out of the prison word

parts.note: the cooler and the nick are both slang for prison
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A king is snubbed by a cooler, more charming queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooler' is not colder here but slang for jail, NICK; drop its K.
explanation.definitionFit: Charming and nice are both words for pleasant, so more charming is the comparative of agreeable.

clue.text: Bill abandoning Spain for Western Australia after a serious conflict

indicators.note: abandoning X for Y says the Spain letter is swapped out for the Australian state

parts.note: a bill is a printed notice or poster
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)
WA is the abbreviation for the state of Western Australia

explanation.surface: Bill quits Spain for Perth after a serious war.
explanation.walkthrough: POSTER loses E and takes WA in its place, giving POSTWAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Postwar describes the period after a war, which is a serious conflict between nations.

clue.text: Lecturer's got through a course in Rome

indicators.note: a lecturer speaks aloud, so his version is how the words sound

parts.note: passed a, as in getting through an exam

explanation.surface: A lecturer has completed a course on Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got through a' is PASSED A, which spoken sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta is the classic first course of an Italian meal, served in Rome before the main dish.

clue.text: Outgoing administration avoids attending game

indicators.note: attending means accompanying, so the avoids word goes beside the game word

parts.note: a game leg is a lame one
to duck something is to avoid it

explanation.surface: The departing government dodges going to the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' as an adjective means injured or lame, as in a game leg.
explanation.definitionFit: Officials serving out their term after a successor is chosen, like an outgoing government, are called by this term.

clue.text: Drunk goes back, clutching large bottlenecks

indicators.note: clutching means the rearranged letters hold the large letter
drunk suggests the letters of the following words stagger into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A drunk retreats, gripping big bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes back' looks like retreating; it is fodder for 'Drunk', giving BOCKAGES around L.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottleneck is a narrowing that holds up traffic or flow; obstructions of that kind are jams.

clue.text: See 3
Suppressing cry of pain, weak-kneed son bawls

indicators.note: suppressing means the cry is held back, removed from the cowardly word

parts.note: yellow means cowardly or weak-kneed
ow is what one shouts when hurt

explanation.surface: A cowardly boy, stifling a cry of pain, howls anyway.
explanation.definitionFit: To bawl is to shout loudly, so bawls means the same as shouts at full volume.

clue.text: Man who wrote religious text finally shortened church service

indicators.note: finally picks the end letter of each of the two words
shortened means the service word loses its final letter

parts.note: evensong is the evening service of the Church of England

explanation.surface: An author of a religious book trimmed a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Louis Stevenson is the man who wrote the novels clued elsewhere in this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, author of Treasure Island and Kidnapped.

clue.text: Instrumentalist, one unable to follow the lead without note?

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the card player goes round the note

parts.words: one unable to follow the lead
parts.note: in card games a player unable to follow suit may play a trump, so is a trumper
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A musician who cannot keep up with the leader, presumably because he has no score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without note' suggests lacking music; 'without' means outside, and the lead is a card led in bridge or whist.
explanation.definitionFit: A trumpeter is a musician who plays the brass instrument with valves and a flared bell.

clue.text: Bore in a French river

parts.note: un is French for a
the Derwent is a river in England

explanation.surface: A tidal bore on a French river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a noun, a tidal wave on a river; it is the past tense of bear. There are several English rivers called the Derwent.
explanation.definitionFit: Bore is the past tense of bear, meaning endured, the same as went through or experienced.

clue.text: Beloved characters (cruelly slain) written out of 14's work

indicators.note: written out of says these letters are removed from the novel's title

parts.note: Treasure Island is Robert Louis Stevenson's pirate novel
cruelly signals that the five letters of slain are muddled, here into the order found in the title

explanation.surface: Favourite characters are killed off brutally and cut from an author's book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cruelly' turns SLAIN into ISLAN, which is taken out of TREASURE ISLAND, leaving TREASURE D. 'characters' means the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something treasured is cherished and dearly loved, the same as beloved.

clue.text: Notice habit journalist confronted

parts.note: an ad is a notice or advertisement
a habit is a garment, as a nun's dress
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A journalist noticed a habit, perhaps a nun's.
explanation.definitionFit: To address a problem or an audience is to face it directly, so to tackle or confront it.

clue.text: A leaflet written after Celtic's fourth draw

indicators.note: written after places the leaflet word after the letter from Celtic
fourth picks the fourth letter of the team's name

parts.note: a tract is a short pamphlet or leaflet

explanation.surface: A programme note was penned after Celtic's fourth draw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw' looks like a tied match; it is the verb, to pull in. Celtic is a Glasgow football club.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a crowd is to pull it in, which is to attract it.

clue.text: King notably had one about breaching barrier

indicators.note: breaching means breaking into, so the about word goes inside the barrier

parts.note: a dam is a barrier across water
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A king famously had something to say about breaking through a barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: King is Martin Luther King, whose 1963 speech began 'I have a dream'.
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Luther King's famous 1963 speech centred on his vision of racial equality, expressed as a hope for the future.

clue.text: Songs by tenor breaking setter's reserve

indicators.note: breaking means the songs and tenor split the possessive word

parts.note: the setter speaks of herself, so the setter's is my
odes are lyric poems or songs

explanation.surface: Songs by a tenor break down the setter's reticence.
explanation.definitionFit: Reserve in a person is restraint and reticence, a self-effacing quality much like humility.

clue.text: Relish country's leader moving to the right

indicators.note: the first letter of the country word shifts rightwards along it

parts.note: a state is a country

explanation.surface: A nation enjoys its head of government shifting politically rightwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of STATE moves two places along.
explanation.definitionFit: A relish for something is a liking for it, and a taste for it means the same.

clue.text: Primarily South American measure Brazil adopted?

definitions.text: Primarily South American measure Brazil adopted?

indicators.note: primarily picks the first letter of each word that follows

explanation.surface: A query whether a South American step was taken up by Brazil.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: a dance measure from South America that Brazil took as its own.
explanation.definitionFit: This lively Brazilian ballroom dance, with African roots, is closely associated with Rio carnival.

clue.text: Caught on the hop, jockeys ride with spurs

indicators.note: to jockey is to jostle and manoeuvre, so the letters jockey for new positions

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Racing jockeys ride wearing spurs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jockeys' looks like a noun, the riders; it is the verb, signalling a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: To be caught on the hop is a British idiom for being taken unawares, or startled.

clue.text: Drive on the skew could be a bit of a bloomer

definitions.meaning: in golf, a drive that curves sharply off line to the side

definitions.text: could be a bit of a bloomer
definitions.meaning: a piece cut from a bloomer, a British crusty loaf of bread

explanation.surface: A golfer's errant shot might be quite a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is both a blunder and a long British loaf; it is the loaf here.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf a wayward shot curving away is so named, and a thin cut piece of bread is too.

clue.text: In the case of Rice, short song will show it

definitions.text: In the case of Rice, short song will show it

indicators.note: In puts the cut-short song inside the outer letters
the case of Rice is its outside letters
short means the song word loses its last letter

parts.note: a hymn is a religious song

explanation.surface: Tim Rice's lyrics, set in a short song, will show off his skill with words.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: Tim Rice, the lyricist, uses this device in short songs; and Rice chimes with 23's SLICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyricists such as Tim Rice pair words with matching end sounds, which their songs display.

clue.text: Truce reached by warring cities after navy reduced by half

indicators.note: after places the rearranged cities behind the navy part
reduced by half keeps only the first half of the navy word

parts.note: an armada is a fleet or navy

indicators.note: warring suggests conflict that throws the letters into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A ceasefire is agreed between warring cities once the fleet is cut by half.
explanation.definitionFit: An armistice is an agreement to stop fighting, a ceasefire or truce.

clue.text: Pair breaking verbal agreement here in Belgium

indicators.note: breaking means the pair abbreviation splits the agreement word

parts.note: yes is spoken assent

explanation.surface: A couple break off an oral deal here in Belgium.
explanation.definitionFit: Ypres is a town in Belgian Flanders, scene of major battles in the First World War.

clue.text: Apprentice isn't giving up time in plane, say

indicators.note: in places the shortened word inside the tree

parts.note: the plane is a kind of tree, so 'say' marks it as an example

indicators.note: giving up means the time letter is dropped

parts.note: ain't is a colloquial form of isn't

explanation.surface: A novice pilot refuses to give up time on an aeroplane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plane' looks like an aircraft; 'say' marks it as an example of a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: An apprentice is a learner in a trade, someone still being trained.

clue.text: Spray used in northern river for 24 hours

indicators.note: in puts the scrambled letters inside the river

parts.note: the Tay is a river in Scotland

indicators.note: spray scatters, so the following letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Spray is put to use on a Scottish river for a full day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spray' looks like a noun; it is the anagram signal for 'used'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuesday is a day of the week, and a day lasts twenty-four hours.
